To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the distal radius, a predominantly cancellous site, has a lower bone mass and bone size in the early twenties than in the thirties or forties, and that the mid-radial radius, a predominantly cortical site, has a constant bone mass and size throughout this period of time.

the distal radial site is the most useful predictor of the risk of future fractures and is the most sensitive to the effects of age, weight and height, and that the mid-radial site is the least useful predictor of the same risk, but the most sensitive to weight and height, with age having no effect.

(1) peak bone mass at the distal site of the radius was achieved later (i.e. in the 30s) than that of the mid-site of the same radius, (2) the distal radial site was more sensitive to age, and (3) lean body mass was the most significant determinant of both distal and mid-radial bone mass in pre-menopausal women.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the relationship of anthropometric variables to bone mass.
the determinants of bone mass at two sites on the radius in premenopausa women and the relationship of these determinants to bone mass in other skeletal sites.
the age-related changes of radial bone mineral density (rBMD), bone width (rBW) and bone mineral content (rBMC) in premenopausa women.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
, for both the cancellous and cortical portions of the radius, age is the most significant determinant of bone mass.
age is the most important determinant of radial bone mass, with height being a significant predictor of the cortical bone and lean mass being a significant predictor for the cancellous bone.
the determinants of bone mass are complex and multifactorial, with age being the strongest predictor, followed by body size and lean body mass.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the distal radius, a site with a relatively high proportion of cancellous bone and thus with greater remodeling capacity, has the potential to respond to a wide range of environmental influences, including age, height and LBM.
, in premenopau-sal women, the determinants of the radial BMC and BMD are similar, and that the determinants of bone width are different, and are not as well understood.

the distal radial site, as measured by single-photon absorptiometry, is a good site to assess PBM in Caucasian women, and that the site is also sensitive to the effects of age, height, weight and lean body mass on bone mass.
The main takeaway from our work is that
bone mass at the distal radius, which is largely cancellous tissue, is more sensitive to changes in body composition than bone mass at the mid-radial site, which is mostly cortical tissue.

the radial mid-shaft is not the best site to use to assess bone mass and density, especially for women, as the distal site, which is more cancellous and therefore more sensitive to estrogen deficiency, is a better site to use to monitor bone loss.
age and height are the two most important predictors of radial bone mass, with age having a stronger influence on the largely cancellous distal site and height on the mostly cortical mid-site.
